subject: Onramp paths: recommendation and pilot plan (Peering vs PrivateLink vs S2S)
messages:
From: Stephanie Nguyen <stephanie_nguyen@redwood.ai>
To: Carlos Ramirez <carlos.ramirez@acme-analytics.com>, netops@acme-analytics.com
Cc: Ben Carter <ben_carter@redwood.ai>, Laura Bennett <laura_bennett@redwood.ai>
Date: Fri, 27 Nov 2026 09:12:00 -0800
Subject: Onramp paths: short recommendation + info we need

Hi Carlos / Acme NetOps,

Thanks for the call this morning — quick follow-up with a concise framing so we can land a pilot. Acme's goals we heard: low operational change, predictable latency for inference (99th P95 target ~80ms for single-request lookups), and strict auditability for control-plane calls. Based on our internal review we have three realistic onramp patterns to evaluate for Redwood Private (VPC / on-prem):

1) Direct VPC peering (account-to-account peering or peering across Acme VPC and Redwood Private VPC)
   - Pros: native routing, no per-request proxying, lower per-packet overhead. Good for high-throughput, low-latency workloads when IP ranges don't overlap.
   - Cons: cannot be transitive (peering mesh complexity), requires Acme to expose routes into our VPC, and IP management is brittle if ranges overlap.

2) Interface PrivateLink (AWS Interface Endpoints / NLB-backed endpoints)
   - Pros: customers keep their CIDR intact, traffic goes to endpoint ENIs — minimal routing changes and strong isolation. Simpler security model (service policies + SG controls). Works well when you want single-service exposure and limited blast radius.
   - Cons: per-hour and per-GB costs on endpoints/NLBs, connection scale considerations (concurrency), and slightly higher egress latency compared to an ideal peered path.

3) Site-to-site VPN (IPSec tunnel from Acme on-prem or VPC to Redwood edge VPN gateway)
   - Pros: faster to stand up for on-prem and when peering not permitted; strong encryption in transit.
   - Cons: throughput/HA depends on appliances and provisioning (might need active/active tunnels), potentially higher latency and jitter, and more operational overhead.

Visible trade-offs we still need Acme to confirm:
- Expected sustained throughput for inference requests (RPS) and burst patterns (help us size load-balancers / endpoints).
- Any overlapping RFC1918 ranges between Acme VPCs and Redwood's private VPCs (if overlap exists, peering is not feasible without NAT).
- Compliance needs: do you require that control-plane traffic flows over a dedicated tunnel or that we present a single audited endpoint?

Attachment: onramp-options-compare-v1.xlsx has a compact comparison matrix we put together.

Proposed pilot: spin up PrivateLink + a small NLB-backed interface endpoint for the inference control-plane and data-plane (read-only traffic) for 2 weeks. If we hit either scale or latency limits, switch to a peering/tran sit gateway pattern for the production cutover.

Request: Can you confirm the throughput numbers and whether Acme legal will accept a PrivateLink endpoint model for the initial pilot? Also please share any IP-range overlap constraints.

Thanks,

Stephanie Nguyen
Sr. Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference
stephanie_nguyen@redwood.ai
+1 415-555-0142
Redwood Inference

From: Carlos Ramirez <carlos.ramirez@acme-analytics.com>
To: Stephanie Nguyen <stephanie_nguyen@redwood.ai>
Date: Fri, 27 Nov 2026 11:04:00 -0800
Subject: Re: Onramp paths: short recommendation + info we need

Thanks Stephanie — useful summary. Quick answers and clarifications from our side: 

- Throughput: for our first tranche we expect ~120 RPS steady, bursts to ~2.5k RPS tied to customer batch jobs (10–15s bursts). Latency SLO: 95th under 120ms, 99th under 220ms; we know this is tight for remote inference.
- IP planning: our primary VPC (vpc-prod-1) uses 10.3.0.0/16, split across multiple subnets. We do have some legacy DCs using 10.2.0.0/16. Redwood's private VPC using 10.3.0.0/16 would conflict with our prod VPC — so direct peering without NAT is not possible unless we renumber.
- Compliance: our security team prefers a model that provides per-endpoint access auditing and the ability to revoke access quickly. They also want to avoid broad route injections into our VPC.

Given the IP overlap and compliance ask, PrivateLink looks appealing for the pilot. That said, can you share typical latencies you observe (p95/p99) for a PrivateLink + NLB path vs a peered path in the same region? Also, what's the expected operational cost of endpoints at our expected throughput?

Cc'd: netops@acme-analytics.com for visibility and any network constraints.

— Carlos
Head of Platform Engineering, Acme Analytics
From: Ben Carter <ben_carter@redwood.ai>
To: Stephanie Nguyen <stephanie_nguyen@redwood.ai>, Carlos Ramirez <carlos.ramirez@acme-analytics.com>
Cc: Laura Bennett <laura_bennett@redwood.ai>, Rafael Mendes <rafael_mendes@redwood.ai>
Date: Mon, 30 Nov 2026 10:17:00 -0800
Subject: Re: Onramp paths: short recommendation + info we need

Thanks Carlos — good context. A few data points from our side to help the decision: 

- Measured latencies (AWS us-west-2, same AZ tests) from recent PrivateLink tests: p95 ~14–20ms added from client LB to Redwood NLB -> service ENI; p99 ~45–60ms under moderate load. For peered VPC flows in-region (no transit gateway), p95 ~8–12ms; p99 ~28–35ms. These are relative deltas — your absolute numbers will also include application processing cost.
- Cost: PrivateLink has NLB + endpoint hour and per-GB charges; for your projected traffic (120 RPS steady, 2.5k RPS bursts), we estimate ~0.5–1.2TB/month transfer for control/data-plane during early ramp. Ballpark endpoint cost could be ~$800–$1,800/month depending on NLB capacity and cross-AZ charges; we'll refine after we see actual traffic patterns.
- Operational: PrivateLink wins for minimal routing changes (fits Acme compliance preference). It also isolates exposure to just the service interface (good for audits).

Recommendation: Pilot with PrivateLink for 2 weeks as Steph proposed. In parallel, run a synthetic test harness that simulates the expected burst profile to validate p99 under load. If p99 latency under PrivateLink is unacceptable, pursue a staged peering path using a Transit Gateway with route table controls (this reduces the peering mesh pain and allows more controlled route propagation).

Action items I will own:
- I'll drop a prebuilt load script and terraform module for NLB+PrivateLink endpoints into the shared drive by EOD.
- Rafael, can you enumerate the firewall rules we should expect (ports, ephemeral ranges) and confirm whether we need to request any egress exceptions?

— Ben
Principal Solutions Architect, Redwood Inference
From: Stephanie Nguyen <stephanie_nguyen@redwood.ai>
To: Carlos Ramirez <carlos.ramirez@acme-analytics.com>, netops@acme-analytics.com
Cc: Ben Carter <ben_carter@redwood.ai>, Laura Bennett <laura_bennett@redwood.ai>, Rafael Mendes <rafael_mendes@redwood.ai>
Date: Mon, 30 Nov 2026 16:42:00 -0800
Subject: Re: Onramp paths: short recommendation + info we need

Carlos / NetOps — thanks for the quick turnaround and the IP clarity. Next steps and pilot plan: 

1) Proceed with PrivateLink pilot: Redwood will provision an NLB-backed interface endpoint exposing the inference service and control-plane endpoint. Expected pilot window: 2026-12-06 -> 2026-12-20 (two weeks).
2) Load testing: Ben will provide the load harness and terraform by 2026-12-01 so Acme can run synthetic bursts prior to pilot start.
3) Firewall rules: Rafael — please send the minimal port list (we generally need 443 and ephemeral outbound ports; details in attached architecture-sketch-vendor-links.pdf).
4) Fall-back: if p99 latency or scale issues surface, we will evaluate Transit Gateway peering as a production path and schedule a topology workshop week of 2026-12-13.

Please confirm acceptance of the pilot dates and if Acme can provide an initial test account with a non-overlapping ephemeral CIDR or a NAT path for the test harness.

Thanks all — I'll circulate a short mutual action plan doc after I get Rafael's ports and Carlos' confirmation.

Best,

Stephanie Nguyen
Sr. Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference
